extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and typesetters working on book or journal production
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and technical rules for preparing, typesetting, proofreading, and indexing book- and article-length manuscripts, including table composition, spacing, indentation, proofs, and house proofreading procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing names with compounded prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefix compounded with the name: (examples: Vanderkinde, Zurlauben, Dechambre, Vanderhoeck, Delacroix). In the case of the exceptions above noted, the first letter of the prefix governs the alphabetical position of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a name includes a compounded prefix treat the first letter of the prefix as governing alphabetical placement unless an exception is explicitly noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umlaut handling in names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names spelled with the umlaut a, o, u should be listed as if the umlaut were spelled out ae, oe, ue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List e.g. Müller as Muller (or Muller -> Mufola, etc. in the examples). Apply the expanded-vowel form for alphabetization and listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing names joined by connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Names having two parts, or names of firms, connected by 'and', '&', 'y', 'et', 'und', 'e' should be listed according to the first letter of the name preceding the connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Smith & Evans' under 'S'; 'Gomez y Pineda' under 'G'; 'Loubet et Meunier' under 'L'; 'Duncker und Humblot' under 'D'; 'Sandrone e Vallardi' under 'S'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table typography: type size and lead/solid settings
rubrics_metrics.description: In n-pt. and lo-pt. matter open (unruled) tables should ordinarily be set in g-pt. leaded; ruled, in 8-pt. solid. In g-pt. matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 8-pt. solid. In 8-pt. matter open tables should be set in 6-pt. leaded; ruled, in 6-pt. solid. In 6-pt. matter both open and ruled tables should be set in 6-pt. solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the prescribed combination of body type size and whether a table is open or ruled to choose the appropriate table type size and whether lines are leaded or solid. (The section lists concrete pairings for common type measures.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiating numeric columns in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a growing practice of using different type in tables for columns representing totals, averages, percentages, and generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italic and black-face figures to set off various classes of results (e.g., totals vs. percentages) where propriety requires distinguishing columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions and box-heads size and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for the columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables with box-heads of several stories, the upper story — primary heads — should be set in caps and small caps; the lower — secondary — in caps and lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where small caps are used in box-heads, the stub (first column) head should also be set in caps and small caps as a rule. If a second story consists of figures only, follow the exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between rules and enclosed table matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and, if practicable, at least the equivalent of an en quad of the type in which the body of the table is set between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain readable breathing space between rules and table contents: two leads vertically; about an en quad horizontally where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leaders in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders, may be used between the columns. In ruled tables, in the 'stub,' leaders should usually be employed, if there is room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'leader' is a piece of type with dots or short lines used to lead the eye across to the right word/number. Use them to help reader alignment; prefer leaders in stubs of ruled tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank entries and figure alignment in numeric columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders across the full width of the column. Center the figures in the column; if they cannot be put in the exact center and there is an unequal number of digits, leave more space on the left than on the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure visual alignment of numbers; when digits vary, offset slightly to favor left-side spacing so columns appear balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading matter alignment in ruled table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered, if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention, and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center short reading-matter entries; for wrapped lines use hanging indent and left-align wrapped lines for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules usage in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but perpendicularly, as a usual thing, only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double horizontal rules at head of table; avoid vertical double rules unless table layout demands it (e.g., doubled-up tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs ruled table decision by column count
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; of three or more, as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open (unruled) treatment for simple two-column tables; add ruling for three-plus columns to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table headline and descriptive line formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I,' etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following (descriptive) line, if any, in caps and small caps of the same type. A single (descriptive) headline, not preceded by the number of the table, should be set in caps of the type in which the table is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number line in same caps as body type; use caps+small caps for descriptive sub-headline. Single-line descriptive headlines get caps of body type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: point and pica measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica. A pica is twelve points (one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the point/pica system when specifying sizes and indents; understand common names for sizes (pica, small pica, long primer, bourgeois, brevier, minion, nonpareil, pearl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Type style names and manuscript indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman; type with sloping face is called italic; type with a heavy black face is called bold face. In manuscripts italic is indicated by a straight line under the word(s), bold face by a wavy line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark manuscripts with the indicated proofing conventions for italic/bold to communicate desired type style to compositor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomy of type and font components
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of a type is called the shank; the upper surface bearing the character, the face; the part projecting beyond the shank, the kern; the part of the shank projecting beyond the face, the shoulder. A font includes caps, small caps, and lower-case letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know terminology to communicate with compositors and to understand font capabilities (caps, small caps, lower case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard spacing between words and after punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Space evenly. A standard line should have a 3-em space between all words not separated by other punctuation points than commas, and after commas; an en quad after semicolons, and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em quad after periods, and exclamation and interrogation points, concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these spacing norms when justifying and setting copy to produce consistent and readable spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting spacing: order of adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas, and letters of slanting form (large 'shoulder'); if necessary to increase, begin with overlapping letters ('kerns') — straight-up-and-down letters, and points other than periods and commas (in this order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tightening or expanding lines prefer altering spaces around less visually disruptive characters first to preserve appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion rule for a well-spaced line
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line, with a 3-em space between a majority of the words, there should not be more than an en quad between the rest; this proportion should be maintained in increasing or reducing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain proportion of most-common spacing to occasional wider spaces to avoid ragged or uneven-looking lines; to justify a line is to adjust spacing making it even or true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alternating extreme spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if at all avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep visual consistency across adjacent lines to avoid distracting variation in spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: No hair-spacing or em-quad to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially compress or over-expand a line to force fit; prefer acceptable line breaks or other editorial adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line of paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing of an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expanding the last line to create excessive trailing white space at paragraph ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing around short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words, like 'a,' 'an,' etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure equal spacing around small function words to preserve evenness of text color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin space after certain symbols and before abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, ¶, and similar signs; before '£.,' 'ff.,' and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply narrow spacing conventions around legal/abbreviation and metric symbols for typographical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency and numeric symbol spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols $, and £ (pounds), s. (shillings), and d. (pence), and the numerals (an en leader is used for a decimal point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write $2.75; £1035.2d; 10° C with no space between symbol and number, and adhere to the prescribed decimal mark convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals in headings and small caps
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines denoting subsections, there should be an en quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em quad. Small-cap headings should have an en quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified quads/spaces after numerals and between heading elements to maintain consistent heading rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture reference spacing convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced thus: II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5 — 3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the example format for biblical citations, using punctuation and spacing as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: No spacing between letters in products and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write product notations and superscripts/subscripts tightly adjacent to base letters (e.g., ab, x^2) without added spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules by measure and type size (plain paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of from 10 to 20, indent n-pt., 10-pt., 9-pt., 8-pt. 1½ ems; 6-pt., 2. In measures of from 20 to 30, indent n-pt., 10-pt., 1½ ems; 9-pt., 1¼; 8-pt., 2; 6-pt., 2½. (This is for plain paragraphs.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the numeric indent amounts according to measure width and body type size for consistent paragraph indention. (The manual gives a full table of specific values.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules for hanging indentions
rubrics_metrics.description: In hanging indentions, in measures of less than 10 picas, indent all sizes 1 em; from 10 to 20, n-pt., 10-pt., 9-pt., and 8-pt., 1½ ems; 6-pt., 2 ems; from 20 to 30, n-pt., 10-pt., 9-pt., and 8-pt., 2 ems; 6-pt., 3 ems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified hanging indention amounts when first line is set flush and the remaining lines are indented; follow the table for precise em values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry indentation and alignment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let the indention be governed by that; where quotations from different poems vary slightly in length, indent all alike; indent according to rhymes and length of lines; in blank verse align lines; align consecutive rhymes; if rhymes alternate indent the rhyming lines alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For poetic set-offs choose alignment and indents to achieve a centered appearance governed by longest lines; align lines with consistent rhyme/pattern-based indentation as illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs and when to use hanging indention
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable. Where it is desired to bring into relief the opening word or words of a paragraph, or the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines, 'hanging indention' is often employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain paragraphs for readability; reserve hanging indention for emphasis or when formatting multi-line center-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and standard thickness of lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type. The ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads between the lines is called leaded; without, solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify 'leaded' or 'solid' in typesetting and use the 2-point standard lead as a default unless another leading is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of slug and its standard sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: A slug is a strip of metal, thicker than a lead, used in the make-up of printed matter into pages, to be inserted after headlines, etc. The two standard sizes are 6 and 12 points thick, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slugs to add vertical space after headings or in make-up; select from the standard sizes as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof types and terminology (galley, page, plate, foul, revise)
rubrics_metrics.description: A galley-proof is an impression of the type contained in a galley; a page-proof is an impression of the type material made up into page-form; a plate-proof or foundry-proof is a proof taken of the type-page immediately before an electrotype cast is made; a foul proof is a galley-proof containing author's corrections; a revise is a new proof of type corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct proof names to communicate stage of production and expected level of correction; expect foul proofs to include author marks and revises to reflect marked corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up, folio, drop-folio, and half-title definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The arranging into page-form of type-lines is called the make-up. A folio is a page-number (even on verso, odd on recto); a drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page. A half-title or bastard title is an abbreviated title on a separate page preceding the full title-page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these conventions for page numbering and preliminary-title placement in book design and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype vs linotype spacing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype composition uses an unit system (18 units in a quad) with cast 'fixed' spaces (6-unit standard, 5-unit, 4-unit), and swelling (justifying) space added on keyboard; linotype uses the pica system with three fixed spaces (em quad, en quad, thin space) and a space band to spread spaces to sizes between a 3-em space and slightly larger than an en quad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing copy, be aware that linotype and monotype machines handle spacing differently, and that slight changes in linotype-set lines may require resetting whole lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript physical preparation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be either typewritten or in a perfectly clear handwriting (typewritten preferable). Sheets should be uniform size (9"x11" desirable). Only one side of the paper should be used. Never roll manuscripts; place them flat in a box or envelope. Sheets should not be fastened together except by pins or clips. Use mucilage, not pins, when fastening a piece of a page to another. Liberal margins should be left at top and left-hand side. Pages should be numbered consecutively. Inserted and omitted pages should be clearly indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these physical handling and labeling conventions to avoid loss/damage and to give compositors/proofreaders room for marks and instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions for indicating inserts and omitted pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheets to be inserted after p.4 should be marked '4A', '4B', etc.; sheets omitted between p.4 and p.8 should be indicated by numbering p.4, '4-7'. Additions to original pages should be placed after the sheets to which they belong and should be marked 'Insert A', 'Insert B', etc., with the insertion point indicated in the margin of the original pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified labeling scheme to communicate where inserts belong and to avoid misplacement during make-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and footnote indications in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated either by indenting the first line or by a ¶ mark. Footnotes should be clearly designated (e.g., separated by a line or using different-color ink); the word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark paragraphs and notes clearly to prevent compositor/proofreader confusion; use superscript figures and keep notes distinct from body text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering convention for linotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Number footnotes consecutively throughout an article or by chapters in a book; bear in mind that in matter set on the linotype machine the slightest change necessitates the resetting of the whole line, so renumbering throughout is costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer consecutive numbering across the article/chapter but be aware of linotype resetting costs when changing numbers late in production; monotype or hand-set matter is less sensitive to numerical changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading: returning proofs and using standard marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return your proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets, use the standard proofreaders' marks (do not adopt your own system). Answer all queries in proofs. Remember that changes in the type cost money; make manuscript as perfect as possible before delivering. Alterations should be made in the galley-proof; corrections in plates should be avoided. The original manuscript should be returned with the galley-proof; each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, consistent use of standard marks and careful attention to queries reduces errors and cost; always supply prior marked proofs and manuscript to support queries and cost accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreaders' professional responsibilities and approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you yourself were the author. Be particularly careful about proper names and figures. If the copy is not perfectly clear or if you doubt correctness, look it up or query the author. Make queries clear; be discreet about queries; study the 'personal equation' of individuals you work with. Never hesitate to correct anything palpably wrong. Do not follow copy blindly; follow copy only when correct. Do not ask authors or editors to decide questions of style; learn the Manual of Style. Do not shield yourself behind the copyholder. Cultivate speed but accuracy is more important. In unavoidable rushes protect yourself by noting limits. Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the proofreader's role as the arbiter of typographical correctness within the house style; balance speed and accuracy; document your work and questions clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholder duties and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading voice; small words are as essential as big ones — get them all in and right. Enunciate plural 's' distinctly. Do not be offended when asked to repeat. Regulate speed; do not guess at a word — examine context. Sit at right angles to your reader. Slow up the moment the reader marks corrections. Evolve your own system of signals. Do not waste time over matters of style (the proofreader knows the rules). Be careful in transferring marks. When sending proofs, ensure everything is there; arrange copy and proof-sheets neatly and consecutively. Consult the job ticket for number and recipient; manuscript should accompany galley-proof; foul proof should accompany page-proof (or manuscript if no galley proof was sent). Indicate contents of envelopes; fasten pins at top center; return volumes to file each evening. Keep proof-room neat and records organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these operational, communication, and housekeeping practices to minimize errors and speed the proofreading/setters' workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard proofreader's marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard marks such as 'dele' (delete), letter reversed (turn), put in (insert), close up (no space), bad spacing (space more evenly), wrong font, transpose, make a new paragraph, indent, carry left/right, elevate, imperfect type—correct, space shows between words—push down, straighten crooked line, query to author, put in capitals/small capitals/lower case/roman/italic/bold face, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the conventional set of proofreader's marks (the manual lists symbols and their meanings) so compositors can unambiguously execute corrections; do not invent idiosyncratic marks.
